transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-23
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Ravi Kapoor (Redwood SE), Ava Torres (Redwood CSM) -- Elena Ruiz (Borealis Head of MLOps), Mark Sato (Platform), Priya Nair (SRE), Tom Briggs (Product)

Summary (auto): quick RCA recap from last week's 5xx/timeouts, agreed experiments around retry budget and short synthetic burst test; next steps: trace export + config recommendations + cost estimate for dedicated capacity.

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for jumping on, um we'll run through last week's incidents, what we saw in the pilot, and then run though recommended tuning. Ravi's gonna take most of the tech deep dive.
[00:22] Elena: thanks, Jordan. quick note, we had another late spike on Friday, 09:00Z, so Priya put in a ticket — we'll share traces in a sec. overall the app hit some timeouts at the payment service.
[00:35] Priya: yeah, the 504s mostly. it looked correlated to a backlog in the inference queue, and our side's retries just amplified the queues.
[00:50] Ravi: ok, that's consistent with the sample telemetry we pulled. two main patterns: one, short tail latency spikes when concurrency bursts hit a worker and KV-cache misses cause extra decode work; two, a hard failure path where we hit a rate limit and then clients retry with aggressive windows.
[01:15] Mark: when you say "rate limit" is that at the Redwood edge or our own ingress?
[01:22] Ravi: mostly Redwood per-tenant route limits we saw in the headers — 429s were returned after sustained high RPS, and some of them propagated because client code retried immediately, no backoff, so the overall queue grew and created timeouts (504).
[01:38] Jordan: to be clear, the platform also triggered temporary circuit breaking when the backend queue crossed thresholds; that was an intended graceful degrade but I know it still shows up as 5xx to your stack.
[01:52] Priya: yeah that was surprising — we expected 429s but got some 502/503s. transcripts from some apps say 502 at the proxy level.
[02:05] Ravi: sometimes the proxy maps internal circuit break states to 502/503 depending on the language client; there can be name mismatches — we should map the headers.
[02:20] Tom: do you think dedicated capacity would have prevented this? or just reduced probability?
[02:28] Jordan: dedicated would give predictable concurrency limits and isolate your tenant from noisy neighbors. but it doesn't remove the need for proper retry/backoff and client-side throttling. think of it as increasing the capacity ceiling and reducing cross-tenant variance.
[02:45] Elena: we have strict cost constraints too. if dedicated is 3x the hosted price we need to justify it. what are the cheaper quick wins?
[02:55] Ravi: quick wins: 1) set a conservative retry budget on client side (max retries 1-2 with exponential backoff starting 200ms), 2) enable prefix KV cache for repeated prompts to avoid cold-decoding, 3) bump the short-lived concurrency limit per route by a small amount, 4) set a per-route circuit breaker on the ingress so failures fail fast instead of piling up.
[03:22] Mark: on the kv cache — our prompts are slightly dynamic, would that still help?
[03:28] Ravi: yes if you have shared template prefixes or system messages. KV cache helps when the first N tokens are identical across requests. if you don't have those, we can look at micro-batching at the client layer.
[03:42] Priya: micro-batching seems risky for our latency targets. we need p95 under 300ms on most flows.
[03:49] Ravi: understood — then KV cache + tighter retry budget is the better path. also enable the Redwood adaptive backoff flag we discussed — it has a warm-up window to avoid hotkey thundering herd.
[04:05] Elena: warm-up window… can you explain that a bit?
[04:08] Ravi: sure — it basically prevents sending all traffic to freshly started worker until it has warmed its KV cache. traffic is ramped. in practice it reduces initial 5xx during bursty traffic. it's part of the managed runtime, we can enable per-tenant.
[04:25] Jordan: quick interjection — we'll also share a short doc + example YAML for the retry/circuit-breaker policy, so you can drop it into your ingress clients.
[04:34] Tom: great. now on Friday's spike specifically, what did you see in the telemetry?
[04:39] Ravi: I pulled the aggregated metrics: CPU on the workers was fine, GPU utilization spiked but not saturated, what looked odd was the request queue depth for a couple of minutes — it jumped from median 15 to 230 and stayed high for 90s. during that window latency tails and 5xx rose.
[05:02] Mark: 230 queue depth — is that our app or Redwood queue?
[05:06] Ravi: Redwood-side per-tenant queue. we throttled to protect the overall cluster which is why you saw 502/503 in some stacks.
[05:15] Priya: does that mean our clients should be backing off more aggressively?
[05:18] Ravi: yes. we recommend a retry budget that decays on 429/502/503 and a longer base backoff after a 5xx. also implement jitter so retries don't synchronize.
[05:30] Elena: can we get sample code?
[05:32] Jordan: yes, Ravi will post a gist — we'll include curl examples.
[05:36]
[06:00] Ravi: another datapoint — some of the 5xx correlated with large batches of long prompts that forced KV cache misses and longer LM decode time. heuristic: long prompts + no prefix reuse => higher token compute. so during a burst that becomes a multiplier.
[06:20] Mark: if we can limit user-entered prompt size at the edge, would that help?
[06:24] Ravi: truncation/normalization at the edge helps a lot. also token-limit enforcement and early reject when prompt length would push expected latency above p95 target.
[06:35] Tom: are there runtime flags we can enable to queue less aggressively?
[06:38] Ravi: yes, you can lower the cluster's max queue depth per-tenant and enable fast-fail for requests that would exceed estimated latency, but that will increase 429s — which is ok if clients retry politely.
[06:50] Priya: what's the recommended max retries then? 1 or 2?
[06:53] Ravi: for synchronous user-facing flows we usually recommend 1 retry with exponential backoff and capped jitter. for background tasks maybe 2-3. but don't retry on 4xx.
[07:05] Elena: last week we saw retries of up to 10 from a misconfigured client library — that was the noisy neighbor that amplified the issue. we fixed it but the traces still show some residual impact.
[07:17] Jordan: ok, so immediate list: confirm any clients with high retry loops, set retry budget to 1 for front-line calls, enable adaptive backoff and KV cache where applicable, run synthetic burst test.

[10:00] Mark: about the synthetic burst — how should we run it? what's the profile?
[10:05] Ravi: run multiple stepped bursts: 100rps -> 300rps -> 600rps with 30s holds, include your standard prompt mix and also a few heavy-long prompts, and observe queue depth and rate-limit headers. we can run that from Redwood side or you can run it from your infra, we'd prefer to run it as a joint test so we can correlate internal telemetry.
[10:30] Priya: we can open a window next week to run that. we will need the exact script.
[10:35] Jordan: we'll provide the script and also a shared spreadsheet to post metrics.

[12:00] Elena: small ask — can the Redwood console show per-route retry counts and queue size in the UI so we don't always need to pull logs?
[12:10] Ava: that's a fair ask — we have per-route traces and rate-limit counters in the console but the visibility is sometimes limited by retention; we can add a temporary higher-retention view for your pilot.
[12:25] Tom: perfect. also, on the cost side, if we enable a small dedicated fleet for peak windows only, is that supported?
[12:33] Jordan: yes — burst capacity from dedicated is possible, we can propose a hybrid where you keep hosted but reserve small dedicated pool for peak windows. we'll include a cost worksheet.

[15:00] Ravi: quick note on headers — when you capture traces, please include the X-Redwood-* headers (e.g. X-Redwood-Quota, X-Redwood-Queue) so we can map internal events to your traces. sometimes those headers are stripped by proxies and we lose visibility.
[15:20] Priya: ah we do have a proxy that strips some unknown headers by default; we'll change that.

[18:00] Mark: any thought about client-side circuit breaker pattern? we have a sidecar that could implement it.
[18:07] Ravi: sidecar is ideal — implement a token-bucket limiter and a simple circuit-breaker that opens on sustained 5xx > threshold for 60s. that prevents retry storms and keeps the overall system healthy.
[18:25] Elena: what's a good threshold?
[18:28] Ravi: something like 5% 5xx over a 1-minute window is a starting point, tuned down for low traffic routes.

[22:00] Tom: one more question — any chance the model itself is causing heavy decode tails? we've been experimenting with a larger variant this week.
[22:08] Ravi: yes larger models increase per-token decode cost and exacerbate tail latencies. switching to a smaller quantized variant for high-volume routes is a common pattern — Redwood Optimize recommendations can suggest quantization profiles.
[22:25] Jordan: we'll attach the Optimize doc and our quantization notes; if you want, we can run a small A/B where 10% of requests go to a smaller quantized model to measure impact.

[30:00] Priya: timeline/acceptance — we need to be confident the POC meets our SLOs for one week before moving to production. what's a realistic timeline for the suggested changes?
[30:10] Jordan: quick wins (retry config + header retention + console retention bump + KV cache toggle) can be done in 3-5 business days. synthetic burst and analysis 1 week. dedicated cost estimate 2 business days. overall we can have a 2-week readiness window if you approve.
[30:30] Elena: sounds doable. we'll prioritize retry fix and header changes.

[36:00] Ravi: ok I'll share the retry/cb yaml. example:
- max_retries: 1
- backoff_base_ms: 200
- backoff_multiplier: 2.0
- jitter: true
- open_threshold: 0.05 # 5%
- open_window_s: 60
(we will put this as a downloadable gist)

[38:20] Mark: what about observability for retries? we'd like a per-endpoint metric for retry attempts and retry-scope.
[38:25] Ava: we'll enable per-route retry counters and surface them as a chart. we'll also give you a shared dashboard link.

[42:00] Jordan: ok let's recap actions — Priya will share traces for the June 18th spike; Ravi will post retry/circuit-breaker config and the synthetic burst script; Jordan/Ava will run the burst jointly and share the cost worksheet for dedicated/hybrid; Mark will check KV cache usage possibility and Tom/Elena will sign off on acceptance criteria.
[42:28] Elena: agreed. thanks everyone. quick plug — please flag any docs in the shared folder so we can find them easily.
[42:36] Jordan: will do, I'll upload links in the meeting notes.
[42:40] Tom: thanks all.
[42:44] (meeting closes)

References/Artifacts mentioned:

- Shared spreadsheet for burst metrics: https://docs.internal/redwood/borealis-poc-burst (placeholder)
